review.title: Nhận xét bài viết trên lớp
paragraphs: There is an opinion that students having the best academic results should be rewarded; however, others believe that rewarding students showing improvements plays a crucial role. In my opinion, both groups of students should be recognized and rewarded.

Admittedly, rewarding students standing out is needlessly exact. Initially, since students have diligently applied themselves to their studies, they deserve their praises and privileges. This may encourage these students and others to study harder to win the rewards, propelling towards overall academic gains. Furthermore, this kind of competition has be seen in almost every aspect of life, where only the best individuals are rewarded. This means that students are used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition, enable them to achieve success in later life.

However, I believe that students having improved should be also rewarded. Firstly, only a few smart students can come first and receive the rewards, causing others to think that their effort is futile because they can not surpass those outstanding individuals. This prone to feeling overwhelmed and disheartened, gradually losing the incentive to study. Added to this is that emphasizing improvements can encourage all students to be diligent in their studies and help students to understand that they need to constantly improve themselves, irrespective of how well they have been or are performing. It naturally follows that the constant desire to outdo themselves, even benefiting themselves more than the competitive determination to win against all others.

In conclusion, I firmly convinced that both students including outstanding students, improving students or improved ones should be rewarded, which the best way to emphasize their improvements and efforts.

paragraphs: Opinions are divided over whether schools should reward students with the best academic results or whether it is more important to reward students who show progress. I believe that both groups should be recognized and rewarded.

Admittedly, rewarding students with outstanding academic results is reasonable. Since those students have diligently applied themselves to their studies, they deserve their praises and privileges. This may encourage them and other students to study harder, thereby contributing to overall academic gains. Furthermore, competition exists in almost every aspect of life, where only the best individuals are rewarded. Becoming familiar with this reality can help students thrive in the face of fierce competition and may prepare them better for success in later life.

However, students who show progress should also be rewarded. If only a few high-achieving students receive rewards, other students may think that their effort is futile because they cannot surpass those outstanding individuals. As a result, students may feel overwhelmed and disheartened and may gradually lose the incentive to study. Furthermore, recognizing improvement can encourage all students to work diligently and to understand that they need to keep improving themselves, irrespective of their current performance. The constant desire to outdo themselves can even benefit them more than competing against others.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that both students with outstanding results and those who make progress should be rewarded. This is the best way to recognize achievement and effort.

review.title: Nhận xét bài viết trên lớp
paragraphs: It is argued that people can reach historical objects and artworks through computer, so public museums and art galleries are unnecessary. From my perspective, I am the opposite school of thought.

Admittedly, technology have positive impacts in bring efficient historical and cultural experiences. Chief of these is that technology, say, high-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions, virtual reality platforms can enable viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. For instance, one of the most famous museums in the world, Louvre museum, offers opportunity to experience online exhibitions, which accessible to people over the world, helping many people pursue their passion. Added to this is that this suit those who cannot afford or have mobility issues, still access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, I believe that public museums and art galleries remain essential. Initially, online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of feeling an artefact or artwork in person, evoking emotions and a sense of authenticity that digital images can convey. One clear example is Viet Nam, where many museums and galleries have been built to exhibit historical artworks or inventions in the past. Furthermore, museums and galleries as vital cultural hubs, symbolize the identity of a region, It is naturally follows that this as a magnet for tourism and a facilitator of bonding within the community.
In conclusion, I am convinced that even though technological tools bring new historical and cultural experiences for viewers, it cannot replace museums and galleries.

completion.comment: Bài có đủ mở bài, hai thân bài và kết bài.

review.overall: Em viết đủ bốn phần và có đúng cặp ý công nghệ hỗ trợ tiếp cận – bảo tàng vẫn cần thiết. Em có chuỗi công cụ số, ví dụ Louvre và ý trung tâm văn hóa. Tuy nhiên, mức tự soát chưa đạt: 'which accessible', 'this suit ... still access', 'It is naturally follows that this as a magnet' đều là lỗi câu cơ bản; 'digital images can convey' còn đảo ngược luận điểm trực tiếp. Em cần nghiêm túc viết lại các câu ấy, kiểm tra chủ ngữ, động từ và quy chiếu, rồi mới nộp bản sửa.

paragraphs: It is argued that people can view historical objects and artworks on a computer, leading some to believe that public museums and art galleries will no longer be needed. From my perspective, I am of the opposite school of thought.

Admittedly, technology has positive impacts by providing useful historical and cultural experiences. Chief of these is that technology, say, high-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions, virtual reality platforms, can enable viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. For instance, one of the most famous museums in the world, Louvre museum, offers opportunities to experience online exhibitions, which are accessible to people around the world, helping many people pursue their passion. Added to this is that these exhibitions suit those who cannot afford a museum visit or have mobility issues, allowing them to access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, I believe that public museums and art galleries remain essential. Initially, online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of seeing an artefact or artwork in person. Viewing an artefact or artwork in person can evoke emotions and a sense of authenticity that digital images cannot convey. One clear example is Viet Nam, where many museums and galleries have been built to exhibit historical artworks or inventions from the past. Seeing these original exhibits in person can help visitors feel connected to the people and events behind them. Furthermore, museums and galleries, as vital cultural hubs, symbolize the identity of a region. It naturally follows that they can attract tourists and facilitate bonding within the community.
In conclusion, I am convinced that even though technological tools bring new historical and cultural experiences to viewers, they cannot replace museums and galleries.

paragraphs: It is argued that dangerous sports should be prohibited by law; by contrast, others believe that individuals should be free to take part. From my perspective, I am at the latter school of thought, provided that certain conditions are met.

Admittedly, one might argue that dangerous sports should be prohibited. Initially, if even a minor error, can cause a death of a participant with skydiving is a clear example. However, the prohibition is unavailable since these sports often happen in remote locations, say, mountain cliffs, having minimal surveillance and control. Added to this is that it is unrealistic when a police officer follows every individual prevent them from leaving out a place. As a result, a prohibition exists only on drive practice underground, making it harder to ensure basic safety standards.

To add further evidence to my assertion, I note that people should be permitted to do any sports, as long as they understand risks and receive sufficient training. For instance, unsafe sports like deep-ocean diving and bungee jumping should be registered with reputable club, which can provide appropriate equipment and qualified supervision. It is also notable that new participant should be accompanied by an expert and taught what to do when accidents occur, helping them recognise dangers and respond appropriately. It naturally follows that proper training and necessary precautions can lead to safer participation as no activity is entirely risk-free.

In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that banning dangerous sports is neither practical not effective. Therefore, people should have freedom to choose, under strict conditions of training and awareness, which is a more realistic approach.

paragraphs: It is argued that children should be learned through trial and error; however, others believe that adults should help avoid mistakes. Personally, I am of the former school of thought, as children should have freedom to make mistakes, provided that errors do not involve serious danger.

On the one hand, opponents of a trial-and-error approach often emphasize that most mistakes can be avoidable, showing through dangerous things, say, knives, fire, electricity, which is unnecessary to get hurt to learn to be careful. In addition, parents often take responsibility for shielding their children from harm, so forestall their children's mistakes like fulfill this duty. Moreover, pre-emptively helping children with profound advices before doing something also makes their parents become peace of mind, since they consistently do their best to protect and raise their children.

However, those on the other side have their own valid reasoning. Chief among these is that parents cannot be around their children all the time; therefore, it is inevitable to children to experiment with new things and make mistakes. It is naturally follows that these mistakes offer children invaluable lessons, standing children in good stead in later stages of life. This means that they may be shielded from everything, enabling they to grow up overdependent on others, which is an undesirable personality.

Overall, it seems to me that making mistakes allows children to learn from them. This can also prepare for children's future, provided that their parents give guidance on important matters, by preventing errors that may derail their future.

paragraphs: It is argued that children should learn through trial and error; however, others believe that adults should help children avoid mistakes. Personally, I am of the former school of thought: children should have the freedom to make mistakes, provided that the errors do not involve serious danger.

On the one hand, opponents of the trial-and-error approach often emphasise that most mistakes can be avoidable. They point to dangerous things, such as knives, fire and electricity. Children need not get hurt by them to learn to be careful. In addition, parents often take responsibility for shielding their children from harm. Forestalling their children's mistakes helps them fulfil this duty. Moreover, pre-emptively giving children sound advice before risky activities also allows parents to enjoy peace of mind, since they have done their best to protect and raise their children.

However, those who support allowing children to make mistakes have their own valid reasoning. Chief among these is that parents cannot be around their children all the time; therefore, it is inevitable that children will experiment with new things and may make mistakes. It naturally follows that these mistakes can offer children invaluable lessons, standing them in good stead later in life. By contrast, if children are shielded from everything, they may grow up overdependent on others, an undesirable trait.

Overall, it seems to me that making mistakes allows children to learn from them. This can also help prepare children for their future, provided that their parents give guidance on important matters to prevent errors that may derail their future.

paragraphs: The given bar chart illustrates how many tons of three different fossil fuels of greenhouse gas in the UK over a 20-year period, commencing from 1990.
Overall, there was a general decrease in the number of oil and coal in the UK, while the opposite was true in the case of gas.

In 1990, the number of carbon emissions from gas started at 220 million tons, after which it went up dramatically to 300 million tons in 2000. The figures for coal, by contrast, declined significantly between 310 million tons and 250 tons for the same period of time. Almost no variation was observed in the case of oil, despite a slight fall in 1995.

Regarding categories with the latter time line studied, the number of carbon emission from gas continued to grow, by from 300 million tons to 350 million tons in 2010, ranking first of the entire chart. The figures for coal, conversely, went down at 190 tons, at the same time, marking the lowest point of the whole graph. Finally, such a fall in the number of carbon emissions from oil, but to a lesser extent, of 50 million tons between 2000 and 2010.

Tuy nhiên, em đang gọi khối lượng khí thải là number, ghi thiếu million ở hai số liệu, và đọc mức gas năm 2010 thành 350 thay vì khoảng 320 triệu tấn. paragraphs.text: The bar chart shows how much carbon was emitted from gas, oil and coal in the UK between 1990 and 2010. The figures are measured in millions of tons and are given at five-year intervals.

Overall, emissions from gas rose throughout the period and became the highest of the three from 2000 onwards. Coal emissions declined steadily, whereas those from oil fell overall despite a brief recovery around the middle of the period.

In 1990, gas-related emissions stood at about 220 million tons, compared with roughly 270 million tons for oil and 310 million tons for coal. The gas figure then rose substantially to around 300 million tons in 2000. By contrast, coal emissions fell from about 310 to 250 million tons over the same decade. Oil followed a less consistent pattern: its figure dropped to approximately 240 million tons in 1995 before recovering to about 260 million in 2000.

From 2000 to 2010, gas emissions continued to increase, reaching approximately 320 million tons at the end of the period. This made gas the largest source of emissions among the three fuels shown. Coal fell further to about 190 million tons, the lowest figure in 2010. Oil emissions also declined, although less sharply than coal's, from around 260 to 210 million tons over the final decade, a fall of approximately 50 million tons.

paragraphs: It is argued that history play the most important role in school subjects; however, others believe that subjects such as science and technology are more essential in the world nowadays. From my perspectives, both subjects are necessary as school subjects.

On the one hand, it is admitted that history is very important in school. Initially, it allows students to understand about the past, especially the history of their countries, making them to know more about the origin of their countries and ancestors. Furthermore, history also helps students expand their knowledge by not only exploring the wars but also studying the foreign culture and customs in the past.

On the other hand, scientific subjects, likewise, have many optimistic effects on students. Chief among these is that they help students applied in reality, offering more opportunities for them in the future. For instance, subjects, say, Math, Science are used much in our lives, in working and in the same fields as technology or science. paragraphs.text: People disagree about which school subjects should receive the greatest attention. Some regard history as particularly important, whereas others place greater value on science and technology in the modern world. From my perspective, both areas deserve a place in the curriculum because they help students develop different kinds of knowledge and ability.

On the one hand, studying history allows young people to understand the past of their own country and the lives of earlier generations. By learning how their ancestors lived and responded to major events, students can gain a clearer sense of where their society came from. History also exposes them to the customs and traditions of other countries. For example, examining how people in another society lived during a particular period can help students understand why its present culture differs from their own. These lessons broaden their knowledge beyond the events of a single war or nation.

On the other hand, science and technology can prepare students to deal with practical problems. Mathematics, for instance, teaches them to analyse numbers and compare possible solutions. They can use these abilities when planning a budget or working with data in a future job. Technology classes can also give students experience with digital tools that many workplaces now use. When learners apply what they have studied to an unfamiliar task, they practise solving problems independently and may become more confident. Such abilities can widen their choices in further education and employment.

In conclusion, I believe both fields should remain important parts of school education. History helps students understand societies and cultures, while science and technology develop practical skills for further study and work. Their benefits are different, and students need opportunities to learn from both.
